title: Differentiability of product Gaussian averages
statement: Let $I$ be a finite set, and let $f:\mathbb R^I\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $|f(z)|\le 1$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^I$. For every variance $v>0$, the function $m\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R^I}\left(\prod_{i\in I}p_v(m_i,z_i)\right)f(z)\,dz$ is continuously differentiable, where $p_v(c,z)$ is the density at $z$ of the Gaussian distribution with mean $c$ and variance $v$, and the integral is with respect to Lebesgue measure.
replaced: Let $I$ be finite and $v\ge0$. Write $p_v(c,z)$ for the $N(c,v)$ density when $v>0$ and set $p_0(c,z)=0$; define $G_v(c,z)=\prod_{i\in I}p_v(c_i,z_i)$ and interpret division by zero as zero. Let $A_v(c,z)$ be the linear functional $h\mapsto\sum_i\bigl(\prod_{j\ne i}p_v(c_j,z_j)\bigr)((z_i-c_i)/v)p_v(c_i,z_i)h_i$. Let $f:\mathbb R^I\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $|f|\le1$. If $v>0$, the map $m\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R^I}G_v(m,z)f(z)\,dz$ is continuously differentiable.
